statement.p:
We will explore cofactor expansions through some examples.
Using a cofactor expansion, show that the determinant of the following matrix \det \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 2 \amp 0 \amp -1 \\ 3 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ -2 \amp 4 \amp -3 \\ \end{array}\right] = -36 . Remember that you can choose any row or column to create the expansion, but the choice of a particular row or column may simplify the computation.
Use a cofactor expansion to find the determinant of
\left[\begin{array}{rrrr} -3 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 4 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ -1 \amp 4 \amp -4 \amp 0\\ 0 \amp 3 \amp 2 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right] . Explain how the cofactor expansion technique shows that the determinant of a triangular matrix is equal to the product of its diagonal entries.
Use a cofactor expansion to determine whether the following vectors form a basis of \real^3:
\threevec{2}{-1}{-2}, \threevec{1}{-1}{2}, \threevec{1}{0}{-4} .
Sage will compute the determinant of a matrix A with the command A.det(). Use Sage to find the determinant of the matrix
\left[\begin{array}{rrrr} 2 \amp 1 \amp -2 \amp -3 \\ 3 \amp 0 \amp -1 \amp -2 \\ -3 \amp 4 \amp 1 \amp 2\\ 1 \amp 3 \amp 3 \amp -1 \\ \end{array}\right] .

li.p:
We will using a cofactor expanion along the first row so that
\begin{array}{rl} \det\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 2 \amp 0 \amp -1 \\ 3 \amp 1 \amp 2 \\ -2 \amp 4 \amp -3 \\ \end{array}\right] = \amp (-1)^{1+1}\cdot 2 \det\left[\begin{array}{rr} 1 \amp 2 \\ 4 \amp -3 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ \amp + (-1)^{1+3}\cdot (-1) \det\left[\begin{array}{rr} 3 \amp 1 \\ -2 \amp 4 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ = \amp 2(-11) - 14 = -36\text{.} \end{array}

Expanding along the first row gives
\begin{array}{rl} \det \left[\begin{array}{rrrr} -3 \amp 0 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 4 \amp 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ -1 \amp 4 \amp -4 \amp 0\\ 0 \amp 3 \amp 2 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right] \amp = 3\det \left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 \amp 0 \amp 0 \\ 4 \amp -4 \amp 0\\ 3 \amp 2 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ \amp =-3(1)\det \left[\begin{array}{rr} -4 \amp 0 \\ 2 \amp 3 \\ \end{array}\right] \\ \amp =-3(1)(-4)(3) = 36\text{.} \end{array}

We form the matrix A whose columns are the three given vectors. Expanding along either the second row or third column to take advantage of the zero in the (2,3) entry, we see that \det(A) = 0, which means that A is not invertible. Therefore, the vectors do not form a basis for \real^3.
